title: Buddhism: the middle way
hookLine: neither indulgence nor harshness, the Buddha's first teaching (Samyutta Nikaya 56.11)

cards: January. The plan is to change everything: up at five, cold showers, no sugar, no screens, a run every day. By the third week the plan is in pieces, and by February there's cereal straight from the box at midnight.
Then the cycle starts again: too much, then too little. The Buddha knew that swing from the inside. He'd lived both ends of it, the palace and the starving years.
So the first thing he taught about the path was where to walk. Today: Buddhism's middle way.

teach.b: Back to the Deer Park, and the five companions who had watched Siddhartha starve himself, then walked away from him when he ate.
When the Buddha came back to them, the Samyutta Nikaya records, the very first thing he said, even before the four noble truths, was about two extremes to avoid.
One is chasing sense pleasures: low, he says, and not leading anywhere good. The other is tormenting yourself: painful, and just as useless. He'd tried both.
Between them, he said, there's a middle way, which leads to clear seeing, to peace and to awakening.
And he names it: the noble eightfold path. Right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration. The middle isn't lukewarm.

It's balance that works. Another collection, the Anguttara Nikaya, has a lovely story about this. A monk named Sona practiced so hard, walking in meditation, that his feet bled, and still he got nowhere.
He was ready to quit and go home.
The Buddha came to him and asked: before you became a monk, you played the lute, didn't you? When the strings were too tight, did it sound good? No.
Too loose? No. And when they were tuned, not too tight, not too loose?
Then it sounded just right. Effort is like that, the Buddha told him. Too much makes you restless, too little makes you lazy.
Tune it. Sona did, and the texts say he went on to awakening.

how: Buddhists speak of the Buddha's path as the middle way between indulgence and self-mortification, practiced as the noble eightfold path; teachers tell the story of Sona's lute to people who push themselves too hard.

o: doing everything halfway, never fully committing
the path between indulgence and tormenting yourself
a midpoint between two rival schools of thought

games.q: the middle way — tap the pairs.
p: not too tight, not too loose

s: the middle way means doing everything halfway
it's balance that works, walked as the eightfold path.
the Buddha named the two extremes before the four noble truths
in the first teaching at the Deer Park.
Sona reached awakening by pushing harder
he tuned his effort like a lute string, then went on to awakening.

games.q: you're Sona. you've practiced so hard your feet bleed, and you're getting nowhere. the Buddha asks about your old lute. what's the lesson?
o: tune them: not too tight, not too loose.
games.why: too tight and the lute won't play; too loose, the same. the Buddha tells Sona to tune his effort, and the texts say he went on to awakening.

practice: Tune your sitting first: if you're straining, too upright, jaw tight, loosen a little; if you're slumping or drifting, lift a little, until you find the tuned string.
Then pick one habit you swing on, food, exercise, work, your phone, and picture the too-tight version and the too-loose one. Now picture the middle: something you could actually keep.

wordCard.voice: Buddhism's middle way. Neither indulgence nor self-torment: the path between them, named in the Buddha's first teaching. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali: the middle way, the path between two extremes.

carryVoice: Your line: the middle. Not the heroic version, not the collapse, but the one you could keep every day. See you tomorrow.
